See also: Nonheroic Units

Nonheroic characters include everything from professional workers to petty criminals, police officers to common thugs. They lack the inclination or training to be heroes. but they are capable in their own fields. Skilled engineers, educated professors, and master architects are all Nonheroic characters, as is the local governor, the self-serving spice merchant, and the baseline Imperial Stormtrooper.

Nonheroic characters do not gain Talents, do not add their Nonheroic Class Level to their Defense Scores, and do not gain Force Points or Destiny Points. In addition, they only get to increase one Ability Score by one point every fourth level (instead of increasing two scores by one point each). However, they gain Feats normally as they advance in level.

Game Rule Information

Nonheroic characters have the following game statistics.

Nonheroic Leveling Statistics
LEVEL BASE ATTACK BONUS LEVEL BASE ATTACK BONUS
1st +0 11th +8
2nd +1 12th +9
3rd +2 13th +9
4th +3 14th +10
5th +3 15th +11
6th +4 16th +12
7th +5 17th +12
8th +6 18th +13
9th +6 19th +14
10th +7 20th +15

Hit Points

At each level, Nonheroic characters gain 1d4 Hit Points + their Constitution modifier.

Force Points

Nonheroic characters do not gain Force Points.

Class Features

Nonheroic characters receive no special class features other than some starting Feats at 1st level.

Starting Feats

A Nonheroic character gains three starting Feats at 1st level, chosen from the following list:

Armor Proficiency (Light), Armor Proficiency (Medium), Skill Focus*, Skill Training*, Weapon Proficiency (Advanced Melee), Weapon Proficiency (Heavy Weapons), Weapon Proficiency (Pistols), Weapon Proficiency (Rifles), Weapon Proficiency (Simple Weapons).

*This Feat may be taken more than once. Each time the Feat is selected, it applies to a different Skill.

Multiclassing

A Nonheroic character can Multiclass into a heroic class. The normal multiclassing rules apply.

Class Skills

(Trained in 1 + Intelligence modifier, minimum 1):

  • Acrobatics
  • Climb
  • Deception
  • Endurance
  • Gather Information
  • Initiative
  • Jump
  • Knowledge (all types, taken individually)
  • Mechanics
  • Perception
  • Persuasion
  • Pilot
  • Ride
  • Stealth
  • Survival
  • Swim
  • Treat Injury
  • Use Computer

Character Archetypes

The following pregenerated characters are examples of typical allies and opponents that you can throw into an adventure or campaign. They represent some of the more common characters seen across the various Star Wars eras. Add personalities and histories to these archetypal characters as you see fit.

Creating Non-Human Characters

The statistics provided here use the Human Species as the baseline. If you wish to change the character's Species, follow these simple rules:

  • Remove one of the character's Feats. (Human characters gain a bonus Feat).
  • Remove one of the character's Trained Skills. (Human characters gain a bonus Trained Skill).
  • Add the relevant Species Traits for the selected Species.

system.description:
See also: Near-Humans

Humans dominate the Core Worlds and can be found in virtually every corner of the galaxy. They are the ancestors of early spacefaring pioneers, conquerors, traders, travelers, and refugees. Humans have always been people on the move. As a result, they can be found on almost every inhabited planet. As a Species, Humans are physically, culturally, and politically diverse. Hardy or fine, light-skinned or dark, Humans remain one of the most dominant Species throughout all eras of play.

Human Characteristics

Personality: Human personality runs the gamut of possibilities, though members of this Species tend to be highly adaptable, tenacious, and willing to keep striving no matter the odds. They are flexible and ambitious, diverse in their tastes, morals, customs, and habits.

Age Groups: Humans age at the following stages:

CHILD YOUNG ADULT ADULT MIDDLE AGE OLD VENERABLE
1-11 Years 12-15 Years 16-40 Years 41-59 Years 60-79 Years 80+ Years

Homeworlds: Various, including Coruscant, Corellia, Naboo, Tatooine, and Alderaan.

Languages: Humans speak, read, and write Basic. They often learn other languages as well, including obscure ones.

Example Names: Anakin, Arani, Bail, Ben, Biggs, Boba, Corran, Dack, Dané, Galak, Garm, Han, Jango, Jodo, Lando, Leia, Luke, Mace, Mara, Obi-Wan, Owen, Padmé, Qui-Gon, Sia-Lan, Rann, Talon, Vor'en, Wedge, Winter.

Adventurers: Humans aren't afraid to try anything, and Human adventurers are the most audacious, daring, and ambitious members of an audacious, daring, and ambitious Species. A Human can earn glory by amassing power, wealth, and fame. More than any other Species, Humans champion causes rather than territories or groups.

Human Species Traits

Humans share the following Species Traits:

The The Native Tribes affiliation data created by Wikia user Chellewalker (formerly Wikia user Lukewarner).

The Forest Moon of Endor teems with life, including sentient beings such as the Ewoks and their allied Wisties, their distant and more aggressive cousins the Duloks, the hyperactive and mischievous Teeks, the primitive and territorial Yuzzums, and even the far less common Goraxes, Tulgahs, and Zandor Rockers.

Ewoks live in tree-dwelling tribes with gender-based division of labor; males hunt, forage, and make weapons, while females raise young and handle other domestic tasks. Ewok culture revolves around complex animistic beliefs involving the giant trees of the Forest Moon. Maintaining good relations with the Ewoks, Wisties are fierce defenders of their home and allies, capable of burning enemies through their flamelike bodies. Duloks are green-furred bipeds whose society is divided into various tribes, each headed by a king who has proven themselves the strongest or most fierce of the tribe. Shamans and oracles also enjoy some power in the Duloks' religious society.

Scruffy, mischievous creatures that stands under a meter tall, Teeks scavenge and steal using their enormously fast metabolism and lightning-quick speed. Most other inhabitants of Endor don't like Teeks, finding them to be pests. Primitive hunter-gatherers, Yuzzums employ spears and traps for hunting and defense, and they lack industrial technology. While their neighbors live in the trees of Endor's Forest Moon, Yuzzums occupy the forest floor, hunting small rodents. Territorial creatures that follow a strict hierarchy of strength, Quorks are violent adept in warfare against their neighbors.

Towering over the other residents of the Forest Moon, several types of giants prowl the land. The most infamous of these are the colossal Goraxes; rarely seen but always feared, legends tell of such creatures growing above the very treelines, though the majority are thankfully "only" as tall as boulders. Phlogs are much more widespread and sociable, but their gullible natures and quick tempers still put them at odds with other residents of Endor and they hold a particular hatred for Goraxes.

Isolated from much of the Forest Moon, the communities of Titterbugs and Mudgubs are in a constant struggle with the aggressive and arrogant Gorphs who block their access to potential allies. And with the semi-sentient Fftssfft and Grass Trekkers similarly encroaching on the Gupins, significant regions of the Forest Moon remain disconnected from one another. But while Jinda and Strutter traders are a ubiquitously welcome sight to those more connected communities, the prevalence of Skandit raiders that comes alongside them is far less enjoyable. Similarly contained to a specific region of the Forest Moon, Lizard Warriors dwell near the great lakes and marshes thanks to their semi-amphibious biology. Ketes and Tromes both live in the badlands, the former constructing spawning hives to house their communities and the latter engaging in extensive displays of martial prowess.

And residing in a primitive castle of stone, the Forest Moon's most recent arrivals are that of Sanyassan marauders, whose raw brutality is bolstered by the mystical prowess of Charal the Witch-Queen. These stranded pirates have proven themselves a menace to the other tribes of Endor, with their roaming hunting parties being feared by Ewoks as the "Demons from the Dark Star." Still clinging to hope they could escape the Forest Moon's grasp, these marauders are a scourge to those unfortunate enough to live nearby.

Even on the Forest Moon, several different native communities are of notably smaller stature than others. Living in underground tunnel networks alongside their domesticated insects, Fleebogs constantly struggle against larger predators that endanger their villages while Mimphs, a simple people with a fierce culture of hunting, take great pride in the size of their hunts. And hidden amongst the craggy flatlands of their communities, Zandor Rockers appear as nothing more than simple stones, but are nonetheless a prevalent society that has developed in their isolation.

High in the few frosty mountains of Endor, with the guidance of the Snow King to aid their communities, a number of different tribes call these snowy regions their home. The Ice Demons have carefully cultivated magic rituals they use to prophesize their futures, Iceheads are clever creatures that have learned to navigate their frozen mountains with ease, and the Frostsprites are ambitious tradesmen who are always willing to lend a hand... so long as it puts them ahead as well, of course.

The prevalence of Totem Magic on the Forest Moon has also led to the superstitious reverence of a number of different groups. The Tulgahs are the most well known of these, skilled healers and fantastical sorcerers that come and go from their hidden villages. Lucksprites are impish beings that can supposedly control the fortunes of those around them, and Eodons are said to contain great magic in their beatifical tusks.

Native Tribe Heroic Units

See also: Heroic Units

NAME CHALLENGE LEVEL AFFILIATION NOTES
Web Enhancements
Wicket CL 3 Wicket's trap expertise contributes to the Ewoks' surprisingly effective tactics against their foes.

Native Tribe Nonheroic Units

See also: Nonheroic Units

You are considered Trained in a new Skill.

Effect: Choose one Untrained Skill from your list of Class Skills. You become Trained in that Skill.

Special: This Feat may be selected multiple times. Each time you take this Feat, it applies to a different Class Skill.

system.description:
See also: Feats

You are proficient with a particular kind of weaponry.

Effect: Choose one Weapon Group. You are proficient with all weapons of the selected group. Weapon Groups include the following:

  • Simple Weapons (includes Simple Weapons (Melee), Simple Weapons (Ranged), and Grenades)
  • Pistols
  • Rifles
  • Lightsabers
  • Heavy Weapons (includes both Heavy Weapons and Vehicle Weapons)
  • Advanced Melee

Normal: If you wield a weapon with which you are not proficient, you take a -5 penalty to your attack rolls.

Special: You can gain this Feat multiple times. Each time you take the Feat, it applies to a different Weapon Group. You cannot take Exotic Weapons as a weapon group; instead you must select the Exotic Weapon Proficiency Feat to gain proficiency with a specific Exotic Weapon.

Additional Weapon Proficiency

Reference Book: Star Wars Saga Edition Knights of the Old Republic Campaign Guide

Combined Feat (Quick Draw): You can draw and ignite your Lightsaber as a single Swift Action.

system.description:
A Quarterstaff is made of wood, plasteel, or a metal alloy. A user can strike with either end of the Quarterstaff, taking full advantage of any openings in an opponent's defenses.

A Quarterstaff is a Double Weapon. You can attack with both ends of the weapon as a Full-Round Action, but both attack rolls take a -10 penalty; certain Feats and Talents can reduce these penalties.
